metadata.grounding_note: Questions emphasize practical blockchain infrastructure, custody and abstraction tradeoffs, selective fit, provenance, and real-world implementation risks while avoiding brand, date, and report-metadata trivia.

lectures.title: Blockchain in the Real World - lesson slides
Blockchain in the Real World - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A user clicks a button in a dApp to swap tokens and assumes they are interacting directly with the blockchain itself. What is the best correction to that assumption?
questions.correct_answer: The user is interacting through interface and infrastructure layers that translate intent into signed transactions and chain queries.
incorrect_answers: The user is interacting only with smart contract code because dApps remove wallets, RPC providers, and indexers from the flow.
The user is interacting mainly with a local wallet balance cache that writes the swap result to the ledger after approval.
The user is interacting with validators directly, which sign and submit the swap after the interface records the intent.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames real blockchain use as mediated by wallets, dApps, exchanges, RPC providers, indexers, and other abstractions. These layers shape what the user can do and where risks or failures can appear.

questions.question_stem: Which sequence best describes how a simple wallet action becomes accepted blockchain state?
questions.correct_answer: The wallet creates and signs a transaction, infrastructure broadcasts it to nodes, nodes validate and propagate it, and block producers order it into the ledger under consensus rules.
incorrect_answers: The dApp records the requested swap, an indexer packages it for nodes, validators add the user signature, and the wallet displays the new state after local confirmation.
The wallet prepares a request, an RPC provider signs it for the user, nodes store it as pending state, and indexers order it into a block for consensus before settlement is shown.
The wallet signs a message, an oracle confirms the user's balance, bridge relayers route it to validators, and nodes accept it after dashboard updates are synced to users.
questions.explanation: The transaction pipeline runs from user intent to wallet signing, RPC or node broadcast, validation and propagation, block production, and eventual accepted state. Each layer has a distinct role.

questions.question_stem: A learner says, "My wallet stores my coins, so losing the wallet file deletes the assets from the blockchain." Which response is correct?
questions.correct_answer: A wallet manages keys and signs transactions; assets are recorded on the ledger, but losing key access can make them unusable.
incorrect_answers: A wallet stores a spendable copy of each token locally, so losing the device removes those coins from the public ledger during sync.
A wallet mainly backs up the ledger account at a provider, so losing a file matters only when the provider also fails during recovery.
A wallet holds encrypted balances on the device; losing the password changes the account balance to zero after synchronization on-chain.
questions.explanation: Wallets are control layers, not containers of coins. They manage private keys and authorize actions over ledger-recorded assets, so compromise, loss, or mistaken signing affects control.

questions.question_stem: A newcomer wants easy password recovery and customer support, while an experienced user wants direct control with no platform able to freeze access. Which comparison best captures the custody tradeoff?
questions.correct_answer: Custodial services improve convenience and recovery by delegating key control, while self-custody increases autonomy but makes key loss and signing mistakes more severe.
incorrect_answers: Custodial services keep the user in direct key control while adding support, while self-custody shifts signing and recovery duties to the platform operator.
Self-custody reduces platform dependence by sharing keys with a recovery provider, while custodial wallets leave users solely responsible for seed phrases.
Custodial services mainly differ in interface design, while self-custody offers the same customer support and recovery paths without platform control for most users.
questions.explanation: The lesson avoids ranking custody models as universally safe or unsafe. Custody choices move control, recovery options, platform dependence, and irreversible responsibility to different places.

questions.question_stem: A popular wallet app depends on a single RPC provider. During an outage, users cannot see balances or submit transactions through the app even though the blockchain network is still producing blocks. What does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: RPC providers make node access usable, but dependence on them can become an availability and visibility chokepoint.
incorrect_answers: RPC providers are the wallet custody layer, so an outage prevents private keys from authorizing transactions for users.
RPC providers act as block producers for apps, so an outage pauses ordering even if peer nodes are online elsewhere.
RPC providers are indexers for historical views, so an outage affects dashboards but not transaction submission paths.
questions.explanation: Apps often use RPC infrastructure rather than running their own node access stack. That improves usability but can concentrate dependence for reads, transaction submission, and user perception of network availability.

questions.question_stem: In a blockchain network, why is it misleading to say that nodes and validators always do the same job?
questions.correct_answer: Nodes verify, store, and relay network state, while validators or miners are responsible for ordering transactions into blocks under the consensus process.
incorrect_answers: Nodes mainly keep local copies for applications, while validators or miners alone check transaction validity before every relay step and network propagation.
Nodes mainly forward wallet requests without checking rules, while validators or miners store the ledger and answer application queries for ordinary users and dApps.
Nodes serve RPC users and light clients, while validators or miners define wallet permissions and account recovery policies for the network accounts during use.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes maintaining and checking state from producing blocks and participating in ordering. Honest nodes can still validate rules even when they are not block producers.

questions.question_stem: A lending smart contract liquidates positions when an on-chain price feed reports a sharp price drop, but the feed was delayed and did not reflect the current market. Which concept best explains the failure mode?
questions.correct_answer: Oracles connect smart contracts to external information, so their reporting, aggregation, update timing, and dispute design can directly affect contract outcomes.
incorrect_answers: Indexers shape how applications read historical contract events, so a delayed dashboard index can change liquidation logic on-chain for borrowers and lenders during stress.
Bridges carry asset representations across chains, so delayed relay messages are the source of this contract price input even though the feed is on-chain.
Layer 2 sequencers order transactions before settlement, so stale base-layer batches are the main cause of this price-feed error rather than oracle updates.
questions.explanation: Deterministic smart contracts cannot simply query the web. They depend on oracle mechanisms for external data, and stale or manipulated oracle inputs can cause incorrect on-chain behavior.

questions.question_stem: A portfolio dashboard shows a user's historical token transfers instantly, but one displayed transfer is missing because the dashboard's data pipeline is behind. What should students infer about indexers from this scenario?
questions.correct_answer: Indexers make chain data searchable and application-friendly, but they are derived read infrastructure rather than the canonical ledger.
incorrect_answers: Indexers serve a canonical copy of balances to applications, so their delayed view overrides raw chain records until resynced for users and wallets.
Indexers improve wallet signing performance, so a missing transfer means the transaction was not authorized locally by the wallet.
Indexers replace direct node queries for finality, so dashboards should treat indexed history as the source of truth for apps.
questions.explanation: Raw blockchain data is not optimized for fast application queries. Indexers transform blocks, logs, and events into usable views, but the chain remains the source of canonical state.

questions.question_stem: A user bridges an asset from Chain A to Chain B. The interface says the asset has moved, but the mechanism actually locks assets on Chain A and issues a linked representation on Chain B. What is the main takeaway about bridges?
questions.correct_answer: Bridges enable cross-chain use by adding lock, relay, verification, mint, or release mechanisms, which also introduce additional trust and security assumptions.
incorrect_answers: Bridges make assets native on both chains by copying ledger state, which reduces wrapped-token dependence once minting finishes and relayers report completion to users.
Bridges are mainly indexers that display linked balances across chains while the assets remain on the original network and no representation is issued.
Bridges solve liquidity fragmentation by treating native and wrapped assets as interchangeable under one consensus process across both connected ledgers.
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that separate blockchains do not natively share state. Bridge designs can improve interoperability, but wrapped or linked assets add validation, custody, liquidity, and failure risks.

questions.question_stem: A city department proposes using blockchain for an internal database controlled by one office, with no need for public auditability or coordination across independent parties. How should the proposal be evaluated using a blockchain-fit framework?
questions.correct_answer: It is a weak fit unless blockchain properties solve a real coordination, auditability, or limited-trust problem that a simpler database cannot address.
incorrect_answers: It is a strong fit because immutability is useful for any database, even when one office controls every write, read, approval, and recovery path for the city.
It is a strong fit if the department uses a permissioned chain, because permissioning by itself creates multi-party trust for internal records.
It is neutral until the system adds a public token, because token economics determine whether the records are auditable across agencies.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents blockchain value as selective. The costs and dependencies are more defensible when multiple parties need shared state, auditability, or reduced reliance on a single operator.

questions.question_stem: A pharmaceutical supply chain involves manufacturers, shippers, pharmacies, and regulators that need to trace a drug batch across organizational boundaries. Why is this a plausible blockchain provenance use case?
questions.correct_answer: Multiple parties need a shared, auditable history of origin and handoffs without relying entirely on one recordkeeper.
incorrect_answers: One regulator can keep a private spreadsheet, so blockchain is useful mainly because it hides handoffs from firms and regulators.
Each firm can post separate records, so provenance works without common data standards or coordination across firms.
The drug batch is digital, so a blockchain can verify its physical condition without outside data capture at upload time.
questions.explanation: The reading frames provenance as knowing an item's origin and history. Blockchain may help when goods, credentials, rights, or assets move across parties that need shared records and limited trust in a single operator.

questions.question_stem: A farm uploads a false origin record to a supply-chain blockchain, and the record later becomes difficult to alter. What does this scenario reveal about blockchain provenance?
questions.correct_answer: Tamper-resistant records can make later changes detectable, but they do not guarantee that the original off-chain data was truthful.
incorrect_answers: A ledger can verify farm events at entry, so false records become less likely once validators approve the block from the producer record.
A ledger fixes poor source data through later immutability, so provenance quality improves after enough confirmations on-chain.
A ledger makes altered histories easier to spot, so verifiers should treat the original data as correct by default afterward.
questions.explanation: The reading repeatedly distinguishes auditability from data quality. Hashing and replication can protect the record after entry, but trustworthy provenance still depends on data capture, verification, standards, and participant behavior.

questions.question_stem: A government credential system needs known issuers, selective visibility, efficient validation, and privacy controls rather than open anonymous participation. Which blockchain design principle best applies?
questions.correct_answer: A permissioned or consortium blockchain may fit better because real deployments often need controlled read, submit, or validate rights.
incorrect_answers: A public permissionless blockchain may fit better because open validation usually supplies selective visibility by default.
A private single-operator database is the same design choice because credentials can be copied among agencies through exports.
A public chain with anonymous validators fits best because privacy controls mainly come from hiding issuer identities from credential verifiers.
questions.explanation: The reading separates public/private from permissioned/permissionless dimensions and notes that enterprise, government, identity, and supply-chain systems may need known validators, access control, privacy, and governance.
